ECE 6390 / RF links

Bandwidth & noise

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how wider bandwidth admits more noise while changing the ideal information capacity.

For white input-referred noise, N = kBTsysB. At fixed total carrier power C, increasing equivalent noise bandwidth B increases noise power and decreases C/N.

The ideal additive-white-Gaussian-noise capacity is 𝒞 = B log₂(1 + C/N), in bit/s. Bandwidth and signal-to-noise ratio therefore have to be evaluated together.

A real filter must also pass the wanted signal. Reducing bandwidth can remove information-bearing signal energy or introduce distortion, even while it removes noise. The capacity expression is an upper bound under its specified channel assumptions.

Example

For the normalized teaching case C = 1 W and N₀ = 1 W/Hz, B = 1 Hz gives 1 bit/s capacity. At B = 2 Hz, SNR falls to 1/2 while capacity rises to approximately 1.17 bit/s.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. At fixed carrier power and white noise density, doubling bandwidth changes SNR by how many decibels?

    Noise power is proportional to bandwidth.

    SNR falls by approximately 3.01 dB because noise doubles. Throughput cannot be inferred from that SNR change alone; the available bandwidth also doubled.
